WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : More than 120 US lawmakers raised concerns on Thursday about Alphabet's Google unit acquiring defunct carrier Spirit Airlines' internal data for $10 million to train artificial intelligence systems. The lawmakers led by Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Steven Horsford said the sale would include 100 million emails, 500 million Microsoft Teams messages and other employee records. The lawmakers asked the company to "exclude employee information from the transaction to the greatest extent possible."

Source: Reuters

WASHINGTON, Oct 8 : The four leaders of US President Donald Trump's AI task force are slated to meet on Thursday, task force vice chair Scott Kupor told Reuters, adding that he expects the full committee to convene next week as pressure builds on Washington to take action on AI. The task force is expected to help shape the administration's approach to AI at a pivotal moment for the technology.  Public uneasiness with AI, and the small group of people who seemingly hold sway over it, has risen in recent months. Most US voters think Trump's administration and Congress are not taking the risks of AI seriously enough and want the government to write new regulations for the technology, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Wednesday.  The AI companies "need to step up and demonstrate that they are taking concerns that people have around security and vulnerabilities very seriously, as do we," Kupor said.

Kupor said he expects the group to release a charter outlining its goals and responsibilities after its first full committee meeting. The group will have four to five staff members who will be assigned to the committee full-time, he said. Trump has dubbed the group the Super Intelligence Task Force, using his preferred term for artificial intelligence. It is led by Intelligence Director Jay Clayton, with Kupor, Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson and Defense Department technology lead Emil Michael. Trump calls the Defense Department the Department of War. Kupor said he will focus on engaging industries outside the technology sector, including banking, healthcare and utilities, to better understand how AI could affect their exposure to cyber threats. Michael will work directly with AI developers, Kupor said.

Source: Reuters

(Removes extraneous word 'the' from penultimate paragraph) By Mark Gleeson DURBAN, Oct 8 : Australia’s 2018 ball-tampering scandal is back in the spotlight as the test side return to South Africa for the first time since “Sandpapergate”, but captain Pat Cummins on Thursday dismissed suggestions that Usman Khawaja’s autobiography could trigger further fallout when it is published next month. Australia’s 33-year-old test skipper was one of the bowlers who played in the March 2018 test at Cape Town where Australia were caught using sandpaper to scuff up one side of the ball in an illegal effort to produce prodigious swing.

It sparked a major crisis for Cricket Australia, but only captain Steve Smith and batsmen David Warner and Cameron Bancroft, who was caught with the sandpaper in his pocket, were banned for their part in the scandal. The bowling quartet of Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied any knowledge of the incident. All four are back in South Africa for the three-test series, the first in South Africa since the scandal, which starts at Kingsmead on Friday. Cummins confirmed he has spoken with Khawaja, who was also in the Australian team at Newlands eight years ago. “Didn't go back into too much detail. He just basically gave me the heads-up that he's doing a book, and yeah, as always, no worries. Tell your story. It's fine,” Cummins said. Australian media have reported that Khawaja had urged the team to take collective responsibility at the time of the scandal but the suggestion had been shot down. Cummins said he did not know about the contents of the book. “You need to ask him,” he said. “It’s obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times. So, yeah, it was dealt with then. Now all I can say is, as a group, we moved on, very happy with the last eight years, how we’ve been as a group and evolved.” South African broadcaster SuperSport, whose cameras caught the offending Australians, has poked some fun at the 2018 scandal with a clip on social media that shows Bancroft using the sandpaper on the ball and Australia's reaction after being caught red-handed eight years ago.  In the social media post, the broadcaster warned: “Our cameras will be sharp for this 3-match test series.” (Editing by Pritha Sarkar)

Source: Reuters

Oct 8 : Revolut would favor a primary listing in the United States if the digital bank decides to pursue an initial pubic offering in the future, CEO Nik Storonsky told Bloomberg TV on Thursday. Storonsky, who founded Revolut, told Bloomberg TV that the firm wants to "dominate" the US market and plans to roll out credit cards and loans, once it receives a full banking charter. Revolut received preliminary approval for a national banking licence in the United States in September, after getting licences in Britain and France earlier this year. The bank has risen to become Europe's most valuable startup, having grown rapidly since it was launched just over a decade ago as a fintech promising cheaper forex fees. Valued at $115 billion privately, Revolut is now worth more than Britain's Barclays  and France's Societe Generale. The company's top boss had previously told French newspaper Les Echos the bank was looking into a dual stock market listing in New York and London. Any eventual listing is still likely to be at least a year away, with past media reports citing 2028, and subject to market conditions.

Source: Reuters

Oct 8 : Everton forward Martin Sherif has been fined £5,000 ($6,600) after admitting to breaches of the Football Association's betting regulations over a 15-month period, the FA said on Thursday. The 20-year-old, who is yet to make a senior appearance for the Premier League club, admitted responsibility for 61 bets being placed on soccer matches between November 20, 2024 and February 12, 2026. "The player admitted breaching FA Rule E1.2 by causing, permitting, or enabling 61 bets to be placed on football matches," the FA said in a statement. In mitigation, Sherif maintained he had not personally placed any of the wagers.

Oct 8 : Southampton manager Tonda Eckert said he had accepted responsibility for his role in the club's "spygate" scandal and welcomed the clarity provided by the verdict ahead of Sunday’s south-coast derby against Portsmouth. Eckert was handed a suspended six-week ban and a £28,000 ($36,979) fine after admitting he authorised the observation of training sessions of three rival Championship clubs last season. The FA charged Eckert in July and an independent regulatory commission imposed the sanctions following a hearing, with the governing body confirming on Wednesday that the ban would remain suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season. "I made a mistake and I said that relatively quickly and then I think you just have to accept the consequences," Eckert told reporters on Thursday.

"The only thing for me was to give my version of the story and I'm happy the commission listened... I'm very happy we go into Sunday, one of the biggest games of the season, with clarity. "And that's not just for me, that's for everyone involved in this football club." Eckert acknowledged that he could have faced a much heavier punishment and said the decision allowed Southampton to draw a line under the affair. "There was a fair chance that the verdict goes a different way. After such a long time, we've had a verdict from the EFL, we've had a verdict now (from the FA). "Whatever you expect is not necessarily what you get in the end, so for me it's to hold my hand up one more time." Southampton were expelled from last season's Championship playoff final and deducted four points for the 2026-27 campaign after observing Oxford United, Ipswich Town and Middlesbrough in training. Southampton are 13th in the Championship with 10 points from eight matches. ($1 = 0.7572 pounds)

MOSCOW, Oct 8 : Russian technology and AI company Yandex said on Thursday it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data centre hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored. Yandex said earlier that the attack on its Sasovo hub, one of its five large data centres, caused a fire and forced it to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers. "The scale of the damage to the infrastructure is still being assessed," Yandex said in a statement. "For the moment, we cannot confirm whether it is possible to restore the data centre equipment in Sasovo." The company earlier said some of its services were unavailable and specialist teams were at the site assessing the damage. Two of Yandex's three supercomputers, used to develop its AI model, are housed at the Sasovo data centre. Yandex has not said whether they were damaged.

Source: Reuters

The future of European basketball is in the balance, with the NBA saying it is keen to move forward with its NBA Europe project in 2027 whether a deal is reached or not. The current premier competition in European basketball, the Euroleague, has said it is open to collaborating with the NBA but voted on Tuesday against accepting an NBA proposal. With the Euroleague pressing ahead with its own expansion project, the window is narrowing on any deal before the European basketball landscape shifts. If no deal is found, NBA Europe and the Euroleague would enter direct competition.

City have appealed against the independent commission’s verdict, insisting the judgment contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact." Asked what his message was to supporters ahead of what should be a combustible Premier League match at Liverpool on Sunday, Haaland called for unity and positivity amid the off-field turmoil. LAUSANNE, Switzerland, Oct 8 : A speedy resolution to Senegal's appeal after being stripped of the Africa Cup of Nations title has been promised by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, who heard arguments on Thursday and will have a decision in days. Senegal are contesting the Confederation of African Football's decision to declare Morocco champions, despite Senegal beating the hosts 1-0 after extra time in January's final in Rabat. Senegal walked off the pitch for 14 minutes after a penalty was awarded against them late in regulation time, with several players returning to the dressing room in protest before they resumed play.  Morocco failed to convert the spot kick, sending the match into extra time, where Senegal scored the winner to secure victory.

However, they were stripped of the title two months later after CAF's Appeal Board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match by walking off the pitch, overturning the result and awarding a 3-0 victory to Morocco.  Senegal quickly followed with an appeal to sport's highest court CAS, which was lodged on March 25 but heard on Thursday. "I know it's a long wait for the fans a few months after the final between Senegal and Morocco,” said CAS Director General Matthieu Reeb. “The timetable and the procedural calendar were established with the agreement of the parties involved in this case. So everybody knew about the timeline, and our objective as CAS, as the last instance authority, is to provide a reasoned award as soon as possible after the hearing today,” he told reporters. The long-running saga over the winner of this year’s Africa Cup of Nations title will be concluded within days although Reeb did not give a definite date. “I expect the decision to come not today, not tomorrow, but a few days later. The facts are set, are clear and the discussions will be on some procedural issues and legal aspects," he added. The CAS panel, presided over by French sports law expert Gerald Simon with assistance from Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli and Hamburg-based attorney and professor of law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas, heard the pleadings of the parties who were represented by their lawyers, with the hearing completed on Thursday. Morocco's delegation did not speak to media. Senegal General Secretary Abdoulaye Sow said they were confident. “But the important thing is that sports law is upheld and that this particular match is put to bed, for the sake of dignity and for Africa,” Sow told reporters outside the hearing, which was held behind closed doors.

BERLIN, Oct 8 : UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin will seek another term as head of European soccer's governing body, removing one of the highest-profile figures from the field of potential candidates to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency in March. Ceferin told the presidents and general secretaries of UEFA's 55 national associations in Berlin on Thursday that he would stand for a final term, reversing his previous decision to step down when his current term ends. The Slovenian said in August he would not stand against Infantino in FIFA's presidential election and confirmed his intention on Thursday to stand for reelection at the 51st UEFA Ordinary Congress in Astana, Kazakhstan, on April 22. "I want to thank the national associations for their trust," Ceferin said. "We have faced extraordinary challenges over the past years, and we have faced them as one team. There is still important work ahead, and I have therefore accepted their request (to stand again)."

SEOUL, Oct 8 : E-commerce firm Coupang said on Thursday it has filed two administrative lawsuits against 620 billion won ($462.75 million) in fines imposed by South Korea's government over a data breach. The US-listed company confirmed the filing in a text message to Reuters. ($1 = 1,339.8200 won)

Source: Reuters
